editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Today is Thursday, May 27th, 2004, and this is the beginning of an interview with Kathryn M. Doody at the Erlanger Hathaway Plaza Office, Chattanooga, Tennessee. Ms. Doody was born on November 15th, 1916, and is now 87 years old. My name is Michael Willie, and I'll conduct this interview. Ms. Doody, could you state for the recording your name and its spelling, please?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: My name is Kathryn M. Doody, K-A-T-H-R-Y-N, M, middle initial, Doody, D-O-O-D-Y.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And during which years did you serve?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And which branch of the service?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Army Nurse Corps.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And what was your highest rank attained there?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Major.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And where were you born, Major Doody?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Eaton, Maryland.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Whereabouts is Eaton, Maryland?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: It's in Somerset County, and about seven or 10, 14 miles from Salisbury, Maryland.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Tell me about your family. Did you have any brothers or sisters growing up?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I had one brother and three sisters.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Older? Younger? Where did they fit in?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I am the youngest.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You are the youngest. You're a baby.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. And I'm the only one left now.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. You were born in Eaton, Maryland. Were you raised there also? Did you spend your formative years there?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And what did your parents do? What did your dad do for a living?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: He was a farmer.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I guess that made you a farmer too, didn't it?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Farmer's daughter.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. That's it. All right. Now, born in Eaton. You spent your formative years there. Did you graduate high school?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And so what do you do after high school? What's next?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: My mother wanted to find something for her daughters to do, to make them something other than farmer's daughters.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And she went looking.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And she went to the hospital in Salisbury and she asked about getting her daughters involved in learning nursing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And my sister and I, Emily, received applications to be filled out for nursing shortly after that. We knew nothing about what our mother had done.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, really.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And we were asking, "How did this come about," and so she told us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And then we got excited about it --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and filled out the application.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And at that time, you have to think about, with -- as far as women working, probably nursing and teaching was about it, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, there wasn't -- there weren't really a lot of opportunities.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. Not for farmer's daughters --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- anyway.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Okay. All right. So you get the application, fill it out. And what next? You're accepted or is it -- is it a qualification?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: We are accepted.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. So now where is the -- where actually do you go to school for this?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: In Salisbury.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: The hospital.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Peninsula General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. The general hospital.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. In Salisbury? All right. And you and your sister are together there? I mean, is it --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- where the -- Okay. So that's got to make it nice for you too, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Comfortable. Did you know anybody else there?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I don't believe we did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So you go to Salisbury General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Peninsula General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Peninsula general Hospital. Got you. All right. And so what's the training like?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, it was a little bit difficult, because we had to be very cautious about everything we did. And it was pretty serious studying --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- to do, and ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were you actually living there or were you living at home in --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. You lived there. And ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Kind of a dormitory-like setting?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You would take classes?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were you actually on the floor too?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- with a practical and --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- theoretical?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So it sounds like a pretty good training --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- at that time. Pretty thorough. How long does the training last?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Three years.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Three years. All right. So this is, then, probably around '34, '35? '36?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: '37, I believe.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: That was graduation time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Got you. Okay. So you get out in 1932. Your sister and you both --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- graduate. And then, what? Did you stay there, or you did start looking for a job?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I was anxious to see the world.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: But we had a doctor that was like a grandfather to the nurses. And he was very anxious as to what they did when they graduated. And his idea was, the best thing you could do was private duty. And he tried to sell me that. Well, I did private duty for a while, but there wasn't enough nursing involved in that. All you did was sort of beautician work for the patients. And so I got a catalog that had all the listing of places in the American hospitals. And you know, there were in all the states and everything. So I'd picked out something like Wisconsin or Oregon. And he kept asking me if I didn't made up my mind yet about what I was going to do. And so, yes, I told him yes. And he said, "What is it?" And I said, "I'm going out to Wisconsin or Oregon." And he said --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Any particular reason -- Wisconsin or Oregon seems like --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Far away.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Anyhow, he said, "Let me give you some advice. On your first trip away from home, always have the amount of money in your pocket to return home. Because you're going to get homesick and run home as soon as you do." And I -- I paid attention to him. I listened.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so I gave up on the far, distant places. And I thought, "Where do I want to go now?" And I decided that -- I had never been to the capital of the nation.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: They had always had a trip from the high schools for the students to take this trip in high school. Well, I thought, this is the time to see it, I suppose. So I picked out a hospital in Washington, D.C. And he told me {clears throat} -- excuse me -- when I decided where I wanted to go, let him know. He would pick up the phone and call and see that I got employed, which he did one particular day. And I picked out Sibley Hospital. And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You said Sibley?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Sibley.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And he picked up the phone, just like he said he would do, and called. And they needed nurses right away. So he told me -- asked me if I could be there by tomorrow, and they would, you know, accept me. And I said, "Well, I have to have a little time to unpack my suitcase." I had just come back from a weekend away. So he said, "Well, when, then?" And I decided that, about three days or so, I would be available to go. So I did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And that's still close enough to home --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- to where you're not --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I can always --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- but you're still away on your own.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you get the best of both worlds. Plus the excitement of being in Washington, D.C --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I stayed in Sibley for three or four months. And they had a doctor there who was a little bit wild in his behavior. He used to take -- rip the shirts off interns in the operating room when they did something that displeased him. And so I was working on a postpartum ward, and I was on night duty at the time. And they had called me and told me they were sending down a patient from the delivery room, and she would need an intravenous. But we never kept those things on the ward at that time. We had to call the supervisor, and she would see that we got the material, whatever it was. So I was on the phone talking to the supervisor about getting this intravenous, and they brought the patient down from the delivery room. And I pointed to the room where she was to go, and the doctor and nurse and attendant took her down there. And while I was still talking to the supervisor -- and it was not gossip or something like that. It was about this intravenous.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It was your job, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. And this doctor came up and he said to me, "Get off the telephone." And so I spoke to the supervisor and signed off. And he said to me, "Young lady, don't you ever continue talking on the phone when I come on the scene." He had said, before that, "Get up off your butt," and, you know, go down to the room where the patient is. So this was the fellow that ripped the shirts off --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- the interns. Well, I wasn't about to accept a doctor talking to me like that, even though I was a nurse. And so when the evening was over, the next morning, I went and spoke to the chief nurse. "I want to resign." And she said, "Do you mind telling me why? We have a hard time getting nurses here to stay." And I told her about this incident. And so she said, "Well, is there anyplace else in the hospital you would like to work, rather than where you are?" And I said, "No." And so she said, "Well, give -- take two more weeks and then let me know whether you still feel that way." So I did. And when I went back, her assistant was at the desk. And when I told her I was there to resign, she said, "Young lady, do you know, when you first -- you resign from one government position, it is almost impossible for you to get another one." And so I just went on my way and went back to see the regular chief nurse, when she was there, and told her I was going to be leaving. And so I did. And I was going to go back to Eaton.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: But one of the patients in the ward, the ward I was working on, said to me, "Don't go back." She said, "Go out to Walter Reed. They take civilians. You don't have to --" I told her -- I said, "I'm not in the Army and I can't get in the Army. They won't accept me." I was too short. And she said, "Well, you go out there. You go -- you go into the Navy. The Navy'll take you." I said, "No, their regulations are the same." She said, "No, they're not." So I listened to her, and I went down to the Naval office in Washington, and talked to them, and they said, "No, if you pass everything else and you're 60 inches," which I was, "we'll take you."

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: So I went down to Norfolk Naval Hospital. And there, you had six months' probation, where they decided whether they wanted you and you decided whether you wanted to stay. And so while I was there, about two months after I had been there, the nurses called me from Walter Reed, and they said, "Get back up here. They've lowered the height regulation to 60 inches." And so I was delighted. And I went to the Navy people, and I said, "I want to resign." And they wanted to know why. And I said, "I have another offer of a position." So I went back to Walter Reed. And this was in June of 1940. And I -- they had me taking the oath of office. And when I got through with the oath, the adjutant who was giving it to me said to me, "Young lady, are you --" he said, "Are you aware that this is serious talk that you've been saying?" I said, "Yes." He said, "Well, you were grinning from ear to ear." And I said, "Well, I'm so happy to be here." And so he accepted that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I -- I stayed. And ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What kind of commitment are we talking about when you go in, as far as time, here? Do you actually sign on for a certain amount of time --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- just until --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: You say the oath of office, and you keep that, and all the other regulations they have --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- for employees. And so I got used to that. And I enjoyed my time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. And this is in June of 1942 --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Well, take me from there.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, this -- I went to Walter Reed, knowing -- I really -- they always put signs up on the bulletin board of places where you can transfer to, you know. And so one day on the bulletin board they had Hawaii. And I thought, "Oh, boy. How I would like to go to Hawaii." And so I signed up for it. And I was chosen to go. And that was in September of 1941.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so I hadn't been there for very long when the bombs descended.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Well, let's -- in September of 1941, when you think about it, we're not at war.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: But there is thought -- I mean, a lot of people think we'll be at war soon, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. Nobody mentioned anything.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Nobody -- nobody really talked about --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: "-- we're going to get --"

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- into it at any time? So you go to Hawaii. And that's really the farthest thing from your mind, anyway. You just want to see --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- Hawaii, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. And I hadn't gotten very far about seeing it --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- when the bombs fell.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Do you remember that morning --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- I do. They woke me up, the noise. And I thought, "What in the world can this be?" 'Cause I never heard any racket that was so profound.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. And where are you actually living at that time? Where are you stationed?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: At Tripler Army Hospital in Honolulu --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- in -- in the nurses quarters.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: So finally, when I couldn't go back to sleep, because I turned from side to side, and nothing -- they wouldn't stop dropping the bombs. And so I got up and I went to the bathroom to do the tooth-brushing and face-washing and stuff like that. And we had a window in the bathroom. It was like close to the sink where you were working. And so I looked out while I was brushing my teeth. And the sergeant that lived in the house next to the nurses quarters ran out of his house in the yard -- to the yard and looked up in the sky, as bewildered as I was. And I said to myself, "Well, if he doesn't know what's going on, nobody knows," because that's what they told me when I came in.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, finally the other nurses starting coming -- getting up.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And could you see anything or could you just hear it?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. We went out in the yard when the other nurses came up, and looked up, and saw antiaircraft smoke up in the sky, and didn't know, you know, still, what it signified. And pretty soon, one of the enlisted men, the driver of an ambulance, ran out of the hospital, and jumped in an ambulance and took off. And so I said, "Well, whatever is happening, there's been an accident, because, here, he's gone." So the more nurses got up and came out, they all suggested one thing or another about what was happening. And one said, "Oh, it's the pilots, the military pilots. Whichever one, Army or Navy, has the duty for the weekend, they make all the noise and racket they can to wake the others up who are sleeping." So I accepted that, you know. And then pretty soon, the night nurse came off duty and she said to us, "Girls, you know what's happening?" And we said, "No. What's happening?" She said, "The island of Oahu has been attacked by the enemy, Japan." And I said, "Shut up." Because she was a person that always had the greatest stories, you know, to relate. And she said, "Don't pay any attention to me. Go turn your radios on." So I went in the room and turned the radio on, and that's exactly what they were repeating over and over again. "The island of Oahu has been attacked by the enemy, Japan." And so I thought, "That means war. What's war going to be like?"

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I was on call because I was working in the operating room. And the phone rang as I'm pondering over there. And the nurse in the operating room said, "Ms. Doody, would you mind coming over to the operating room? They're bringing all these men in from Hickam Field." Would I mind? I'm on duty anyway, supposed to be on call.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so I -- I was all dressed except for my uniform. And I put that on. And I couldn't get that off my mind about the war coming. And I'm still pondering. I couldn't figure out what it's going to be like. So I'm walking across the field to the hospital, and then I remembered the stuff I had seen in the sky. And I said to myself, "What goes up also comes down." So I picked up my feet and I ran as fast as I could, to get under cover.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And then I got in the hospital, into the operating room. They had as many stretchers as they could get in one room. You know, all the rooms were filled up with wounded men. And so they told me which room to go in, and so I got scrubbed up and went in. And we were operating on a fellow that had had a fractured leg above the knee, and they were going to amputate that. So the largest bone I had seen amputated in my health -- in my nurse or --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Career.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- career was a finger or a toe. And I said to myself, "The sound of sawing bone, I don't think I can stand, so I'm going to faint." And I never fainted in my life before. And I turned to get something -- an instrument off the table for the surgeon. And when I turned back, they were taking that leg, above the knee, out of the hospital. So apparently the bone was already fractured -- I mean, severed --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and all they had to do was snip it with shears.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And they came around?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Are you thinking at this time, "This is what war is like?" I mean, this is --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I had gotten my mind off what war is like because I was finding out.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. No. That's what I mean.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, you had a --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You had a first-hand realization --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I don't think I --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- of what war --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- I could stand the sound of bone being sawed. And so then a plane flew over, and we heard the bullets hitting the pavement. And the doctor that was working stuck ducked his head, like that. He said, "That was a close one." But none of it hit the hospital. And I've often wondered, they -- at first they didn't know what to do, except to camouflage the hospital.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And then they were told, "No, you put a red cross on hospitals." And I've often thought later that if the Japanese respected the red cross on the hospitals. Because I don't recall if they dropped bombs on any of the hospitals over there. So anyway, we worked -- we worked until midnight that night. And because of the blackout that you had to have made, they couldn't move anymore or -- move the patients away from the floor where the operating room was. And so they sent us home till the next day. And they warned us that they had brought the soldiers in and they were guarding the hospital. And I found out later that that was the only hospital they ever put guards on. And I presume it was because this hospital was on top of the island connection of -- you know, the ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Communications?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Communications. Yeah. And that's why they --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- had it guarded. And when I went home -- Oh, and they said that, on the way home, we'd like -- we're likely to be stopped by a soldier with a "halt," and we were to give our name and -- I forget whether it was number or what else, but there's some things we were supposed to give the soldier. And so I thought, "Well, this is where I -- I get shot to death, because I'll be speechless when I hear that yell to halt," you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, we didn't run into any on the way home. And so then in the nurses' quarters, it was all dark, of course. And the way I couldn't find where my room was, was by feeling the water fountains. We had one in each end of the building. And I was down to the far end, and so I kept across -- I mean, down the hall, feeling along until I ran into that water fountain. And {clears throat} -- excuse me -- when I did, I went in and went to bed. Well, of course I couldn't go to sleep.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so finally, they had -- we didn't have any air conditioning, and the windows and everything were closed. And so I heard my neighbor across the hall turn over in bed, and so I got up and went over and said to her, "Are you awake?" And she said, "Yes." And I said, "Well, tell me what's been happening today," you know. So I got in bed with her until she reported all she knew about the war --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- going on, and what's happening, and everything like that. And then I got back and went to my bed, and I went to sleep for a while.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. You were probably exhausted too.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: _____+ It's been a long day, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm. To be able to talk to somebody and hear something. And so the next morning, we started all over again, you know, with the rooms being filled with wounded soldiers. And some of them, during the night, had released the tourniquets they had on so they would die. You know, they didn't want to live with whatever wound they had received. So we had all sorts of sad things happening, and ... Then things slowed down. We soon caught up with the wounded people. And there was still war, bombing and stuff like that going on. So we got to go to the club on -- sometime during the day, wearing our uniforms, and dancing over there. And I believe we -- they let us have a drink of wine or something there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: That was what we were to do, to have a little bit of recreation.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. It had been pretty stressful for a little bit, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, pretty --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- pretty tough. But by this time, America is preparing for war. Is that -- is it different being there in Hawaii? Because first of all, you're not really on the mainland; and second of all, you were actually involved in the attack. So is there -- is there more of a bond or more of a sense of nationalism or --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I don't remember having anything like that. I guess I did think about some of the things like that, but mostly we were so busy that -- that that's what your mind was on.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: When you saw some of the nurses that were not in the operating room, you could find out what had happened during the day --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So -- how long does it take for things to kind of get back to normal as you slow down a little bit? Is this a matter of days or weeks?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, when you're loaded, it will take a week or so.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Otherwise, a day or so. (Break.)

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So we're going back to the morning of December -- or the day of December 7th, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: A ____+ meeting?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. The morning.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And there was a high-rated doctor who was giving it. And I think his name was Dr. Ironside. And he had changed his topic that he was going to talk about on Sunday morning, from whatever -- he didn't mention what -- but to surgical trauma. And these doctors were from all over the islands. And they were -- when they got a call from the Army headquarters, after it's known what was happening, to report to the military hospital, all of them, you know, that were there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And's so that's why we were so busy with three or four tables --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- in one room. And they were excellent people. And it was just great to work with them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And luckily enough, you have staffing there for it, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, otherwise you probably would have lost a lot more -- a lot more lives.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, that's an amazing coincidence.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Because a lot of people have also talked about, usually all the ships weren't there at the same time.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It just happened --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- on this day they were. Incredible coincidence. And one more thing we were going to mention. You finished the three-year program, and that gave you -- was it actually an RN, a registered nurse, or was it equivalent to today's RN? Was it actually called a --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- registered nurse?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So the initial part is over. You kind of come down from that. But now the war is -- it's actually getting started. We're trying to get troops together and get ready --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- right? So what does that mean to you there at in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, it was -- things were quieter --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and slower, you know. It wasn't a crash or crush or being so busy-busy.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And then, in -- let's see -- '41, '42 -- '42, I believe, or a little bit more than -- I mean, I don't know how late it was in the year '42 -- they decided that -- {clears throat} excuse me -- we people who had been there on December the 7th, 1941, were seasoned troops --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- so -- and by this time, Hitler had gotten things, you know, opened up for World War II.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so they decided to give us 45 days' leave and then send us over to Europe. Which they did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And -- now, how did you feel about that?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Because before, you talked -- you had said -- you had started out saying, "I want to travel. I want to -- I want to see the world."

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, you know what? I wasn't anxious to leave that group of people that I had been working with.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: But I decided that if I turned it down, that I would be sorry. And if my family ever found out that I had done such a thing, they wouldn't appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: So I went home.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And so you were able to get back to the States. Was that included in your -- in your 45 days, or is it 45 days once you get back to the States?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: It was 45 days once we get back to the States.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And on the -- on the way from the west coast to the east coast, on the train, I sat with an officer who had been over in the other military unit in Honolulu, the one I can't remember the name of. It's, you know what, silly that you can't remember, but that's -- sorry. That's the way it is. And so after I had been home -- And we got assigned at home for a little while, till they got ready to send us to Europe. And so while I was doing time in Norfolk Naval Hospital, that I had gotten assigned to, I got a call from this officer that I had sat with on the train, and he said he was going to be the commanding officer of the field hospital, and he wanted me to be his chief nurse. And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Based on a conversation you had?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I wasn't interested in being a chief nurse. And I told him, I said, "You don't have to make me a chief nurse. Just take me with you," you know, "and I'll be a nurse." And so he went to the surgeon general's office en route and requested me to be his chief nurse. And so I got the notice and -- for the -- I got the transfer to move, to start on this trip over to Europe.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: We met at Ft. Jackson, North Carolina, where we collected the people to make up the amount that you needed to --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: South Carolina, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Okay. And when I got down to Ft. Jackson, he said to me, "I want to let you know, you were one of two nurses that I knew back here in the States. And so the other nurse is on the west coast, and I knew I wouldn't have a chance to get her," so he took me, which was to say to me, "Don't expect too many favors from me now just because I requested you."

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so we had a little training at Ft. Jackson to get everybody acquainted with each other.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And then we got our orders to go to Europe. So we went and were deposited in Great Britain to wait until they crossed the channel.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, how -- how did you get overseas?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Ship.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Had you ever been on the ocean before?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was this your first --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: When I went to Honolulu.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, that's right. You had. Okay. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you're sent to -- where did you go?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: We went to Great Britain.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Where we lived with British families.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And the way they did this was, a military man from Britain met our military man from the ship, and they took him up the streets, and we stopped at each house, where they found out how many occupations they could have for somebody there. They had taken us two years before, where they took a record of who had vacant rooms --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- or beds, to take care of people like that. And so then we spent a month or so in Great Britain --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- with these families. And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was -- I mean, was it in -- I don't know how you describe safe, but was it in areas that were close to where bombing was? I mean, was that a concern to you?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I don't think so. Because we didn't hear any of that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you were living with a family?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And they told us, before we went in the house with these people, not to bother them with wanting this or that or the other thing, you know. And so I kept on my own. I just came home and went upstairs and -- to the bedroom, you know, and went out the next morning to where we were having a unit collection.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And one day, as I was coming home and opened the door, the lady of the house opened the door from the rest of the house, and she said, "Young lady --" they called us "billeties," "Young lady, you are very unsociable," or something like that, you know. You know, "We hadn't visited us with us or anything like that." I said, "Well, we were told not to." Well, she was aggravated with that. She never heard of such a thing. Because they're very polite, the British people.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so after that, we visited. They had me down for dinners and things like that, and we became very good friends.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Which would be much more comfortable, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, you were living there.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: But we couldn't tell them when we were leaving, you know, when we got ready to go over to Germany. And so we had been out for overnight, and had _____ some of our time in Britain, and so we didn't have to make any excuse for not being there. We just took off, you know. And so when they got over to Europe and called back and said where I was, you know, like that, she said, "Well, you didn't even tell us you were leaving." And I said, "No. We're supposed to keep it a secret." She knew that. She understood it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: But anyhow ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Just a polite ____+ aspect. Now, during the training, though, when you go to the training, are you aware that something big is about to happen at any time; they're -- they're planning on making the move to start the push? I mean, is that what you're preparing for?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. I mean, you are aware that there's going to be an invasion.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Well, that's part of the war that you --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I know.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- aren't familiar --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: As --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: As it was getting close --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- I didn't know if you, like, realized that something --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, we crossed the channel on D plus 29.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And it was strange to see the -- what the enemy had done, you know; how the fields looked and everything. But we -- we landed in France in hedge rows. We lived in pup tents between hedge rows.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And after 29 days, they're still not too far away, right? I mean, they've --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. No. The thing of it was, our equipment was -- was on a ship with Patton's armor, and he was going so fast that -- you know, he had choice -- first choice on getting his equipment before we did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so it was several months before we -- we got any equipment to work with.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Do you remember where you landed in France?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I know -- I know we -- the ship landed, you know, when we crossed the channel, and -- oh, what was the name of the beach? Utah Beach?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Utah Beach.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I believe that's what --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. But we moved on across Holland and Belgium and into France, and then --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you're waiting for your equipment to catch up with you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So what were you doing in the meantime?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Very little. But this commanding officer we had was treating us like children. Everything was going smoothly. But these nurses that we had -- and that had discipline of the Army, because they had just joined us, you know --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- right from civilian life.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so he decided that he'd keep them as near prison as he could, you know, so he could keep his eye on them. Because over where he had come from in Hawaii, two of the nurses over there had gotten pregnant, and so he was going to make sure that he'd keep an eye on us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And plus you're in a place where there's probably not a lot of, you know, women around.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Oh, yeah. There's nobody around. And I think, as well as I can remember, that we lived on K rations, you know, because we had no kitchen equipment --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- there or anything, and we -- we just had these boxed foods to eat. And anyway, I got to the point where the commanding officer was so mistreating, I felt, to the nurses, that I didn't want to have much to do with him. 'Cause I was young then and didn't know how to talk to commanding officers. And anyway, one day I was sent for by him to come to the tent where they had the office. That was one pyramidal tent where they kept the records and everything. And when I walked in, he was sitting down. And of course, there was no chair for me, so I was standing up. And he said, "Ms. Doody, I -- I think you are aware of the fact that I have court martialed one officer in our unit," which was the advocate, "and I just want to warn you that you'll be the next in line if you don't change your behavior." And I said, "Colonel, I would welcome a court martial to get out of your unit." He slumped over like this, and finally he raised up, and he said, "Why on earth do you say such a thing?" And I said, "It's because of the way you treat the nurses." And he said, "Why didn't you tell me what I was doing?" And I said, "Colonel, if I had thought for a minute you didn't know what you were doing, I would have been glad to." Well, I got away with that. And after he saw us working, the nurses, after we went to work, he came up to me the first day he visited the tent I was in. And I -- we had 18 nurses in this unit, but we were all -- we were split off into three platoons, so there's only, what, six nurses in a platoon. And he came up behind me the first time he visited us, and he said, "I just want to tell you, you're a sight for sore eyes." Well, he meant that for all the nurses, you know. And so I was glad that he had seen something that he liked about us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And everything went along fine.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, how long does it take your equipment to catch up with you?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: It was some months. I can't remember the time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And -- and the equipment that's there -- Is this a -- is this a mobile unit, then? Are you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You're the first line --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- of the troops coming back.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So that probably means -- How often does -- Does that mean you guys are going to have to stay -- You have to stay pretty close to the lines, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I can't say. But it was -- just any -- any time. I think we were left in one place for a few weeks.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Not any shorter time than that, as well as I can remember.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, do you remember the first time you got -- you actually got casualties coming in after you got set up? Do you remember the -- just the feeling when the casualties start coming in?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I don't remember anything outstanding or specific about that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And we had the emergency equipment, you know, to take care of intravenouses and stuff like that, but not anything to keep them there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: We were mostly fixing the patients so they could be transferred to the larger hospitals.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, I was going to say, triage is probably the most important part of --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- the job.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, let me ask you this: Somebody had mentioned to me that it was understood that if you had actually been overrun by the Germans, then you would have to work for them. Is that -- is that the case?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Well, I've been told that. They said, as I understand, if the Germans pushed the Americans back and took over a hospital and the staff was there, was still there, that they would actually have to --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I didn't hear about any of that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So how -- is it -- is it -- it's got to be stressful to a certain extent, but is it fearful? Are -- do you ever find yourself afraid out there, that -- that you're going to be hurt, or are you too busy to think about it?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: We must have been too busy. The only time I was fearful was the time that I was supposed to be halted by a soldier, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: That's the -- that's the only time I remember that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, since you had three platoons, does that -- three platoons of nurses, does that mean basically that you worked three shifts? Is that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. No. We were separated --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- in the platoons. And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you worked whenever, then.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. And I had to go around and visit them with the commanding officer, you know. And everything was very smooth. The nurses were marvelous. Because none of them couldn't stand the work or face it or anything, or got sick.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And we -- we just didn't have anything critical with the nurses.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I would think it would be -- be difficult especially if you hadn't been in that situation before.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. It was amazing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And I think a lot of these guys -- a lot of the men who come in and talk really talk wonders about how, not -- not only professional the nurses were, but also how caring --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- they were, to -- to a point where they were able to provide that emotional support when they needed it.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Is that trained or is that -- is that just a human part of -- of being a nurse?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I think it's just human, of being a nurse.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. So you're -- you're actually following pretty -- How far from behind the line or how close to the line would you actually -- would you actually be as you were moving in?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I really couldn't say, because -- I couldn't see the lines. But it didn't take them long to get those patients to us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was there ever a time for any relaxation, any time to just kind of rest and get away from it, or, being in that position, were you constantly busy and never had time to ...

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, we -- I think we had time at night, you know. We worked -- some nurse was on during the night, but the rest of us, we were off at nighttime.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I was wondering if there was anything you could do to kind of relieve the stress. Because it had to stressful. Just being a nurse, period, would be a stressful situation. Was there anything you could do to kind of let your hair down and relax, any kind of recreation or just getting together and talking or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, we -- we could do that after -- you know, the day nurses could get together --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and talk. But I think most of the time, we were just -- Well, we did, you know, do that, and then -- then off to bed.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Sleep.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were you writing much? And to whom were you writing?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Just my family.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Did you have a specific boyfriend or -- or was there any kind of a --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- any significant other that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Huh-uh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So you're basically working behind the lines.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you remember in -- in -- say, in December -- are you following behind the lines after December, when the Bulge occurs?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Is there a concern during -- during the Battle of the Bulge, that maybe --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And were there -- were there any -- any men, any casualties, or any specific staff, nurses, anybody that -- that really comes to your mind as somebody who, you think back, look back, as somebody who might have influenced your life or you think about often or you think about? You know what I'm saying?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Anybody that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. I do. But it's just been too far.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Oh, I understand. I do understand. One more question I'm going to ask about this. Were there any kind of practical jokers or anybody who would -- maybe comedians or people who would just try to liven -- liven things up and -- and play jokes or anything that would make everybody loose and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Over in Korea, the soldiers used to sing, "The Commies are coming, yoho, yoho." And -- and one of the places where we were, one soldier made a story about, oh, some kind of horrifying situation, and wrote it home to his mother. And she was just, you know, so upset about it. And the commanding officer heard about it, and so he got after him and told him not to do such a thing again.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Something that he just made up or something that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. He was just thinking of all the horror that he could imagine --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and just wrote it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What a terrible thing to do to your mother.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Okay. So you're following behind the lines, then, and going through France. And then did you actually go into Germany?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And there's no -- I mean, you really aren't in a position where you feel like you're going to be overrun or you're going to be shot or anything? Do you remember seeing any planes going over or anything that really signified the war? You were probably so busy anyway. Do you remember when the war was over in Europe?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. I think I was on a trip to the Riviera, had some time off.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Wow. Now, see, that doesn't sound too bad.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, that's getting close to -- we were in a bigger hospital then --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So when does that happen, then? They pull you -- or the -- they transfer everybody into a bigger hospital? Is that the case? Or is it just you?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. It's wherever they -- the people are, that -- the casualties are, bringing them in --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- you know. And this is -- this is to the bigger hospitals, where the minor ones out in the field --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- transfer them. That's where you keep them to, you know, try and get them --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- back to health again and -- a general hospital. And ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you were working in a general hospital at that time?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. And that's when we were getting time to take a --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: R and R?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: So you went to the Riviera.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, that had to be pretty nice.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: In uniform? Or were you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I believe so.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. And I'll bet you were pretty popular, then. What did you do in the Riviera? Talk to me about that.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Let me see if I can remember. I know it was very pleasant, but I -- I'm sorry. I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No, no. Please. I'm just -- I'm just -- I'm throwing out questions. You answer them --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Well, and that's good because --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- as you can.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- these are things I haven't thought about for a while.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you're at the Riviera and you find out that the war is over, right? Or the war is --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, we were flying into Plagne.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- on our way there, I believe it was. We heard that the war had been declared over.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: In Europe.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. So is there any thought in your mind, uh-oh, you might be going to the Pacific, or is that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I never gave that a thought.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Now, let me get back to another point. You did have a brother, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And was your brother in the war also or --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- was he too old for that?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: He was too old for that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And you're the -- are you the only one in the family, then, that goes out? Your sister was a nurse also, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was -- did -- was she involved in anything or --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- did she go back home?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: She was home. She got married.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I had one sister later on, after the war was over, I believe. My older sister was a WAC.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. So you were representing the family well. You're globetrotting, going all over the -- the place. You're at the Riviera.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And you're -- you are -- you're realizing your -- your -- your feeling that you wanted to see the world.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, it's got to be pretty exciting for somebody --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- at that -- at that time. All right. So you find out the war is over in Europe. And then what does that mean to you at that time? You still have a job to do, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: For quite a while. So you spend your time at the Riviera, and you go back to the hospital. So basically, are you -- did you stay there in the general hospital until everyone's taken care of, or how did --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. I -- they -- they -- I think they considered me a pretty good seasoned person --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- always traveling. Because they sent me -- you know, I was at World War II, and then I went to Korea.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Well, let's -- let's talk about that, then. You stayed, then -- how long did you stay in Europe?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Oh, I guess it must have been '45 or '46, something like that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And then when you come back to the -- when you come back to the States, is there any thought that you want to, like, get out of the service or go into --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- private --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- practice?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It's been good to you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- up to this point --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. I just liked it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. So do you get -- you get a promotion then or how -- how do you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I got one promotion over in Germany. I got promotion to first lieutenant, and then to captain over there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So there's incentive for you to stay in, right? I mean, are you making decent money, then, as a captain?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes. As far as I considered it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. And plus the -- I mean, the job is something you're obviously very good at.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And it gave you a certain status.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Oh, I forgot to say, I believe that in the field hospital, the commanding officer that offered me the -- what's the punishment ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, the court martial?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Court martial. He gave me a Bronze Star.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Later on.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: For --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: For the work I was doing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: For valor.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Isn't that wonderful.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And you deserved it, right? I mean, it's -- Yes. You're humble. But yes, you did deserve it.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I -- it was surprising, you know, to come from him, after what he'd said, but ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. I think you woke him up. You probably deserved a Bronze Star just for waking him up. Hold on one second. (Break.)

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So when you get out of Europe, you're -- come back to the -- come back to the States. And then where -- where are you stationed at this point, or where do you go to work at this point?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I'm not sure.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Are you happy being in the States or are you more than willing now --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- to see the world --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- go anywhere you can?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I was willing to go anywhere.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: But then, you know, I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Puerto Rico.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was it Puerto Rico? Manila? You were in Manila?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. But I was in San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I think I left there and went to Japan. And I was in Japan a short time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: While in Japan, your nephew was there, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I think so. Weren't you, Joe?

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: GHQ. General ______+.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And by this time, you're -- Are you a captain at this time?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So really, you've got, I mean, probably good -- good assignments. Wherever you go, you have quite a bit of responsibility. Is that the case?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, after World War II, I decided that I had to specialize in something, because there -- there were too many things involved with medicine --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- to be transferring from one place to another in the Army, where you go from anything, you know ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so I thought I better train for one specific thing. So I -- I didn't choose anesthesia, the chief nurse did that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And she never told me a thing about it until the -- the person from Washington, D.C. came and was going to interview the person, the student, you know, to be students. And so I said to my friends, "Do you think I could be an anesthetist?" Because it was a kind of a startling thing to me. And they said, "Oh, sure. Sure. Sure. You can do it. You can do it."

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Another decision made for you, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. So I did that. And then -- San Francisco, and then in Tokyo. I know we were wondering about being sent to Korea and Japan when things starting working up that way.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And the -- I forget what position he was in the Army -- came up to surgery one day and said, "You can stop worrying about going to Korea," you know, because they were sending over an evac hospital, and they wouldn't need individuals like us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: At that time, where were you? Were you back in the States or were you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I was in -- Well, no. In Japan.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. You were in Japan.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. And two weeks, I think it was, after he said that, we got orders to go to Korea.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: To go to Korea.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Especially you. Because you had experience, right --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- from World War II, which probably made you a very valuable --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I think they remembered that, every time they needed somebody to go to the war zones.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, and a lot of the women had gotten out of the service, right? Gotten married and --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And so that just made you a very attractive candidate, I mean, as far as --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- as far as having the -- having the -- the experience.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: I've got to tell you something.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. Hold on one second. Yeah. Does this concern you at all or is this just part of the responsibility?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I thought it would have been nice, you know, like they said, that we didn't have to worry about going to Korea.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. But did you -- did you realize at that point also that you were probably the best person for the job? I mean --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You didn't?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Didn't make any difference? Okay. So you get your orders. And what does this mean? From this point on, you start getting equipment together; you start -- Do you -- do you have anything to do with the people that are sent with you, or is that done from -- from a higher --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: They just assign --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. That's -- that's done any way they wanted to assign them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. But did you have any choice as far as if you wanted anybody working with you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Or for you? None whatsoever. It's just your job to get in there and ____+. Okay. So how long does it actually take before you're sent over?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. And at that time, your nephew, Joe, was actually in -- he was in Korea, right? I mean, he was over there. Did you think about that at all?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It doesn't occur to you at all?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I just think that would be the worst feeling, to think that you're working in a hospital, and all of a sudden you see somebody you know come in, you know? That was just -- that would be really tough, or it would be tough to think about. I imagine the worst things -- you know, at times probably even think of the worst thing that could happen. So when you actually get into Korea, you are a mobile hospital, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And what does that mean, exactly? You're -- Is it actually called a M.A.S.H.?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: M.A.S.H. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And what is the responsibility of the M.A.S.H. hospital? What is the point of the M.A.S.H. unit?

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: It's a mobile Army surgery hospital.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: That's where the word "M.A.S.H." comes from.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I just wanted her to say it. So it's a mobile Army surgical hospital. And basically you take the serious injuries on the line? Is that -- is that it? After triage, you take the ones that it's life or death, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Is that pretty much it?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. That's got to be tough. Because you're probably getting guys right off the line -- I mean, right off the lines, right? And -- I mean, does -- How do you deal with the stress of that? I mean, is that just part of the job? You get hardened to that?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. It's just what you were trained to do.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. And you're -- are you dealing basic -- or mainly with anesthesiology here, or are you doing everything?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. Just anesthesia.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you were just doing the -- rendering the anesthesia. All right. Now, does this -- is it any more stressful being in another war and doing this or, once again, is it just part of the job?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Just part of the job.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And are you there for a -- for a tour? Are you there for a year or -- I mean, do you know, coming in, that you're just going to be there for a tour --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- or is it an arrangement --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. Just as long as I'm needed. You know, when they were ready to ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Once again, I've got to ask you -- you probably don't know. But I mean, would you -- in this situation, do you have to move more often? Are you over there for a week or two and then have to pick up and move again?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. It's longer than that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. And around when is it when you're -- when you're actually sent there? Are you sent there, what, '50 ... '51?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I don't really know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's all right. That's all right. Don't worry about it.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: It was late '50.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Late '50. Okay. Do you remember anything in particular about the weather that -- I've just heard about some cold winters there.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Don't remember.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And do you remember about how long you were there in Korea?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: (Shakes head.)

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you remember when you actually met with your nephew?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. He has to tell me. I know I met him, but I don't remember any of it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: He told that story when he ...

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you think at all about Korea? Do you ever think back about the time that you spent in Korea, or is that just a -- just a little part of your life there?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I'll tell you, my memory has just been affected, and so these things, I can't tell you how --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No, no. That's fine. And I think that's what happens when you don't think about something for a long time --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- that it does -- it doesn't have the connections. I don't know how the physiology actually works.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I -- it's -- it's affected my brain --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- actually.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And that's why I -- I can't help it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's -- that's absolutely fine. So you were in Korea. Do you remember about how long you were there in Korea?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Something like two years, I think.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Now, you were probably ready to get out after that time.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You've spent a good portion of your life, actually, in war, right? I mean, compared to most people, or a lot of people, you've been in -- spent a good portion of your life in war. Let me ask you this: Do you -- when you're in this kind of a situation, when you're in a stressful situation, and you're, you know, on the lines, and you're, a lot of times, probably working long hours, does that tend to form really close relationships with people? Do you form close friendships that continue after you get out of the service or after that experience is over?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Usually.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. I mean, were there friends that you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- had made over this that you kept up with --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- for years after you got out of the service? Anybody in particular? Any close friends that you got in touch with after you got out?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Not now.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. So you're in Korea for a few years. And then did you come -- You come back to the States after that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- or do you stay in the Far East?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I was in Puerto Rico.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: In Puerto Rico.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: That's where I decided to retire.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Because the people were so emotional there, and I just -- I don't know. I just thought, "This is more than I want to put up with."

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. I mean, in all fairness, I mean, dealing with war, that's a -- that's something that people should not have to deal with, you know, more than once in their lifetime. You've been through two wars, right? I mean, that's -- that's really tough. Now, is this shortly after the Korean War, then, or is this much later on, when you decided to get out?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I think it was, oh, five or six years afterwards, maybe.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. At this point are you still a captain, or have you been --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I'm still major.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Major. Is there thought now at this time that you can retire -- if you stay in a little longer, that you can retire, or can -- does it make no difference to you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- to retire?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Because after 20 years, you can retire anytime.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And had you been in 20 years at this time?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So this is in the '60s, then.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, what about the Vietnam War? Was there any thought that you were going to be shipped over? Did that have anything to do with your decision to get out at all?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Huh-uh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It had nothing to do with it?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Huh-uh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You just got like it was time to get out?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: It was just the --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It was the right time.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- what I said, the -- the emotional part of it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Okay. So you decided to get out. Do you know what you were going to do after you retire, or does it --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I was just going to be retired.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You were just going to be a --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I was --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- retired?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I was ready to quit.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You weren't going to go to war anymore.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
