sp.p: You weren't going do to that, or as far as dealing with that. I mean, was there any thought that you wanted to go with -- continue with your nursing after that or --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So what did you do after you -- after you retired?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I did a little private duty for some, you know, friends or relatives, and then -- and doctors would call on me sometimes to come in and do a day's work or something like that, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Help them out, you know. I did that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And where were you living at that time? Were you back in Maryland?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I -- no. I was -- oh, yeah. Yeah. I was -- I lived in Laurel, Maryland, and -- what was the other place. Some -- some other place in Maryland, close to Laurel, or near, just kind of a short distance away from Washington, D.C.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you were just doing -- I mean, the -- you really didn't take on a full-time --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- full-time position?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. Huh-uh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Did you join any veterans organizations after you got out of the service, or was that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. What was the regular veterans -- just, you know, veterans in Maryland.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I don't know whether they had the veterans in D.C. or not. I know that what they did do about, something about they moved or -- the Maryland veterans -- I don't know -- remember whether it was just the chapter where I was -- to Virginia.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And -- because it wasn't in D. C. either.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Maybe it was _____.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now -- now, I had actually, before -- Did you -- did you get in touch with any of the -- any of the friends at that point? Were you in contact with anybody that you had served with during World War II or during the Korean War, and keep friendships after -- after all those years, or was that a separate life?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I think I probably did for a while. But at the present time, there's no one.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Right. But I'm just talking about the years --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- shortly after you got out --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- if you kept in contact. Because I wonder a lot, if you're in stressful situations during war time, and then you're put in another -- you know, in just regular, average, everyday life after that, if you kind of lose the -- the common bond or --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Huh uh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- by that -- after that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So what have you done since then? You were living in Maryland at that time. How did you end up back here in -- or here in Chattanooga?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Where I was in the District, where they had told me I had to go into assisted living.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I couldn't afford it, because -- I -- I don't know whether I got the right news or not about it being $4,000 a month.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I talked to the executive people, and they said, "You don't have to worry about affording it. We take care of you --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- you know. But I took that to mean that they took care of you by taking anything you had away from you --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And then -- it was just -- except -- I called Joe, because he was my power of attorney, and told him that I was told I had to go to assisted living and that I would not have anything, you know, left for anybody. And somehow it didn't seem right to me to have somebody doing the power of attorney for you.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Making those decisions, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, no. Not leaving them anything for what they're doing. Because they would have to come all the way from Tennessee up to D. C. because I had my funeral services already taken care of --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and I was going to be buried in the national cemetery.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: But it still -- there was a lot of business to do, you know, and I couldn't see leaving something like that for someone to do and not leaving anything for them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: So I called him and told him, you know, that I had to go into assisted living. He said, "Get down here." You know, "You come down here." So it was all settled right then and there, and that's what I did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Now, how do you -- are you a member of any veterans groups anymore, or the women's veterans group here in --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- Chattanooga? Do you know anything about it? That might be something -- you know, you'd be wanted, very inspirational for that group. I'll get somebody there to get in touch with you at that point. Now, since that time, you were given -- What award were you actually given by the director of veterans affairs, Dr. Principi?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: It was this thing you saw me receiving.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Yeah. I just didn't know what, actually, that -- that distinction was called, and I wanted to --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I'm not sure what it was called either.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Didn't I read it somewhere?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, we shot the picture, because I want to -- I want to show the picture. When we do that --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- we can talk about what it is.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I think it's -- it's -- it's on that ...

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, we'll look at that in a little bit. Now, what about a -- have you -- have you attended any reunions of, like, Pearl Harbor survivors or --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I -- I haven't lately, but I was doing that. Went back to Hawaii twice.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And -- and a couple of other places. But I'm too old to travel by myself.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And I have no friends now. Nobody's -- you know, to go with me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: So I don't -- I don't do any of those things. I'm still a member, but I just don't go to them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Let me ask you this: When you went to -- when you went back and visited Hawaii --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- did you -- did you go to Pearl Harbor? Did you go see the Arizona --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- Memorial?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's got to be an odd feeling, knowing that you were -- excuse me -- so close in proximity to all of the -- the devastation that was going on. I mean, do you think back about how -- how much danger you were actually in at that time?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's interesting. 'Cause I'd be scared to death. I would be absolutely scared to death. During the full time that you were in the service -- and I'd say probably specifically, or more importantly, the times when you were behind the lines in World War II and in the Korean War -- is -- was there anything that you took out of that experience that -- any -- any lesson that you learned or any experience that, looking back, kind of changed -- changed the way you -- the way you lived the rest of your life, or changed your -- any experience that really affected you and really kind of made who you are? Does that make any sense at all?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I think it did. But I can't say -- I can't remember any actual incident --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- that brought me to feel that way.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Well, I think, if nothing else, just knowing that you came from a small, just a rural upbringing, and in that, you know, getting to see the world --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I mean, that's pretty --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- major. I mean, that's --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I -- I have this calmness about not being upset or perturbed --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- about this thing or that thing or, you know, anything new or different to other people. I feel like I've experienced just about everything.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so I -- I am not real smitten by any --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, you're -- you've got perspective, I think is what it is.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Other people have described it as saying, you know, when people have been shooting at you, or in your situation, when you've been that close to the lines, or that -- you know, that close to combat, then, you know, the little pressures of daily life really don't mean a whole lot, you know?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I think I've -- my interests have turned more into Christianity --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- and Biblical things. Because when I retired, I decided -- I thought that -- I didn't know very much about the Bible. I had gone -- been raised, you know, with Biblical parents and going to church, but there hadn't been an understanding --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: -- about it even when I took the baptism. And then I joined the Episcopal church, and I was converted to be the Episcopalian religion, but all I felt about it was, I was a member of that church.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And it suddenly dawned on me, these things. And so I decided that I was interested in finding more out about the Bible. Well, I tried to do it by myself, and it was like I was trying to understand the Greek language.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. The blind leading the blind --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You're only as good as your teacher.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And so I tried to find a Bible study. And I asked several people about one, and I never got anywhere, until one day in the church, we were having a bazaar or something of the sort, and I had a table and some of the members of the church had a table. And I heard one of the ladies talking to someone about church and Bible study and all this kind of business. And so when they finished their conversation, I asked a member of the church, I said, "Where is this Bible study that you're talking about?" And she said, "Washington Bible College." And I said, "Can I join you?" And she said, "We're in a group, and I'll ask them and see if you know, they'll permit you." So she came back later and told me that, yes, I could join them. So I went out to Washington Bible College, to this adult class that was held once a week.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Now, it wasn't for any credit or anything, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: For your benefit.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. And so I really became very satisfied with what I was learning. And I think that has taken my mind off all the other things --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It's, once again, perspective. We keep coming back to it. But it does. It puts a lot of things in perspective, right?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, is there anything else you -- that you can think of that you'd like to talk about? Anything else that we might have missed?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Nope.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Joe, what do you think?

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: I think that -- that it still seems to -- it still continues to amaze me that she came from such a little, teeny town, background, in such a rural community, to be able to handle the things that she's handled.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's what we were just talking about. It is. It is. I mean, I think that it truly is.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: And I think that she hasn't talked about the situations in the tents, when they were bringing the people in, and where her -- what she did and what she saw and she did and how she handled it emotionally for those times.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. And that's -- you know, that -- I've tried.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: I understand. I'm sure you did.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I -- I just can't -- none of this comes back to me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's -- I -- that's totally understandable.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: You remember -- I mean, you remember seeing people coming in with -- you know, badly, severely wounded, because you were giving anesthesia to them weren't you?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And that -- you know, it really is. As long as the -- as long as you've got the -- like the -- you made it through. And that's really tough. A lot -- I mean -- you -- a lot of people did not make it through as -- I guess as well-balanced as you did. I mean, they could -- Really, could you -- could you see that situation -- could you understand people really cracking up under the pressure?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: No. I don't recall any of that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No. But I'm saying --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- you can understand --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- if they did. Because I mean, it takes a strong -- it would have to take a strong person to be able to deal with that on a day-to-day basis. I mean -- and that's a testament to you. That's obviously -- as humble as -- as you are, that's a testament to you; that you are able to -- to really not only make it through, but to kind of rise above. It's -- I think it's a -- it's not something that you can really teach. I'll put it that way. That's a testament to you and probably your family.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: The other problem I've got, I think that what happens too is I think you have to kind of detach yourself and really get into -- to what you've been trained to do and not have your emotions interfere with the training.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: You kind of have to separate those things.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Theoretically, I understand what you're talking about.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Yeah. I had to do that in combat. And I -- I saw guys in my unit that were, I mean, fantastic guys, that were so -- that got so worked up that one guy shot himself in the foot so he wouldn't have to go back into combat.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: That's -- that's -- and I think you have to detach yourself --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's what I mean. I think --

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: -- to perform.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I think theoretically I understand that, but I just cannot --

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: You have to do it --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I've never had --

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: -- emotionally.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I've never had to, so I couldn't -- And I would think you're right. You would have to do it. But every time I've talked to a nurse, I've asked them that, and they always say you just didn't. That's --

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: You were trained to do it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's what you were trained to do it, so ... Anyway, I wanted to leave time at the end to get some pictures on tape. So I want to thank you for taking the time to come down here. Joe, I want to thank you for taking the time to bring her down.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: Sure. A pleasure, Mike.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And I truly --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, I'm sorry. I feel like I've been a --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No. I --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Because I --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I understand that.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: I really can't help this memory business.

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: You -- you stop talking about that memory business or I'm going to get irritated.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It's not --

sp.speaker: Joe
sp.p: You can't be 87 and not remember everything.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And really, the whole point -- I don't want you to feel like you're letting anybody down. I just -- that's what I'm saying. I just wanted you to try to get your memories down. The memories that you do have, I want to get them on tape. And you have phenomenal memories, and this is a great tape. You have nothing to be -- I -- you know, I was just asking you --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- trying to bring out as much as I could. We got a lot. This is a -- an absolutely wonderful interview, and you should be really proud and -- not only of this tape but of the service that you've given our country.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Well, you know, these things that I've forgotten will come back to me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. As soon as you get in the car?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: Not -- maybe not that soon, but they'll come back.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Mary Doody
sp.p: And -- But I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, no. No. You did great. Okay. This is you accepting the Secretary's Award from the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, Anthony Principi.
